Haleigh was reported missing at about 3 a.m. Tuesday. Her father’s girlfriend called 911 after realizing the child was no longer inside the family’s Putnam County residence.

Putnam County Sheriff’s Office Maj. Gary Bowling said investigators had ruled out the idea that Haleigh simply wandered outdoors and now had to proceed on the assumption that she had been abducted. He added that the possible motives for taking a 5-year-old were all disturbing.

No one had been formally identified as a suspect, but police were approaching every person they questioned as a potential suspect. As Bowling put it, investigators were considering everyone.

A national Amber Alert stated that Haleigh was last seen dressed in a pink shirt and underwear. Police planned to deploy aircraft equipped with infrared technology after nightfall Wednesday. Bowling noted that Haleigh was only 5 and was frightened of darkness.

Police said Haleigh and her 4-year-old brother were being cared for Monday night by 17-year-old Misty Croslin, the girlfriend of their father, Ronald Cummings. Croslin told investigators she put Haleigh to bed at 8 p.m. and went to sleep herself two hours later. When she woke at 3 a.m., she said, the girl was gone.

According to CNN affiliate WJXT-TV, Croslin told the 911 dispatcher that the back door of the family’s double-wide trailer was standing wide open and that a brick was on the floor. She explained that the door had not been in that condition when she went to sleep. Putnam County Sheriff’s Office Lt. Johnny Greenwood later told CNN that the brick had been used to prop open the trailer door.

Bowling said Croslin was staying with family members while the inquiry continued, describing the 17-year-old as essentially still a child herself.

Earlier Wednesday, Ronald Cummings made an emotional public appeal for his daughter’s safe return, repeatedly saying that all he wanted was to have his child back.

Haleigh’s maternal grandmother, Marie Griffis, told reporters Wednesday that she feared something terrible had happened. Speaking to CNN affiliate WFTV-TV, Griffis said she could sense that Haleigh was somewhere outside and imagined the girl crying out.

Haleigh’s mother, Crystal Sheffield, also broke down in tears before reporters and asked whoever had the child to return her, saying her only wish was to have her baby home.

Griffis said Sheffield and Ronald Cummings had experienced a troubled relationship and alternated weekends with Haleigh. Sheffield, who lives close to the Florida-Georgia border, had been questioned by law enforcement, police said.

Investigators were examining several possibilities. One part of the inquiry involved determining the whereabouts of 44 registered sex offenders living within five miles of the Cummings residence, Greenwood said. He explained that although the total might appear unusually large, it covered both Putnam and Palatka counties, located on opposite sides of the St. Johns River.

Authorities were giving people interviewed in the investigation the option of taking polygraph examinations, but the tests were not mandatory.

Anyone who may have information was asked to contact the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office at 386-329-0800 or the Florida Department of Law Enforcement’s Missing Endangered Persons Information Clearinghouse at 888-FL-MISSING.

**SATSUMA, Florida — February 10, 2009** — Authorities are searching for 5-year-old Haleigh Cummings, who disappeared overnight from her family’s mobile home in Putnam County, Florida, in what investigators say may be an abduction.

Haleigh was last seen Monday night at the home in Satsuma, about 60 miles south of Jacksonville. Her father’s girlfriend, Misty Croslin, told investigators she put Haleigh and the girl’s younger brother to bed and discovered Haleigh missing at about 3 a.m. Tuesday.

In a frantic 911 call, Croslin told a dispatcher that she had awakened to find the back door open and could not locate the child.

Haleigh’s father, Ronald Cummings, then took the telephone and urged police to respond immediately, saying he had just returned from work and found his daughter gone. During the emotional call, he threatened violence against anyone responsible. The dispatcher repeatedly instructed him not to confront anyone and told him officers were on the way.

The Putnam County Sheriff’s Office said deputies, tracking dogs and search teams were combing the area around the home, while investigators interviewed relatives and neighbors. An Amber Alert was issued for Haleigh, who was described as 3 feet tall, weighing about 39 pounds, with blond hair and brown eyes. She was believed to be wearing pink pajamas.

Authorities said the circumstances were suspicious and that an abduction had not been ruled out. Investigators cautioned that no suspect had been publicly identified and asked residents not to draw conclusions about members of Haleigh’s family.

“We are treating this as a missing child and possible abduction,” authorities said, emphasizing that the priority was finding Haleigh safely.

Haleigh’s parents pleaded for her return. Her father urged anyone with information to contact police, while her mother, Crystal Sheffield, appealed directly to whoever might have the girl.

“Please bring my baby home,” Sheffield said. “She needs her family.”

**Haleigh Cummings Disappearance Remains Unsolved Years After Florida Child Vanished**

**SATSUMA, Fla.** — The disappearance of 5-year-old Haleigh Cummings from her family’s mobile home in rural Putnam County remains one of Florida’s most enduring missing-child cases, marked by a disputed account of the night she vanished, a trailer door reportedly propped open with a block or brick, an extensive Amber Alert and a search that examined numerous possible suspects but produced no arrest.

Haleigh was reported missing before dawn on Feb. 10, 2009, from the home on Green Lane in Satsuma, about 60 miles south of Jacksonville. At the time, she lived with her father, Ronald Cummings, and his girlfriend, Misty Croslin, who was 17.

Croslin told investigators that she had been caring for Haleigh and the girl’s younger brother while Cummings worked an overnight shift. According to her account, Haleigh was put to bed that evening, and Croslin later went to sleep. She said she awoke at about 3 a.m. and discovered Haleigh was gone.

A key detail in Croslin’s account involved the rear door of the mobile home. She said the door was open and that a brick or concrete block normally used near the entrance had been moved so that it was holding the door open. Investigators closely examined the doorway and the block, along with other potential evidence inside and around the trailer.

Cummings returned from work shortly afterward, and authorities were contacted. Recordings of the emergency call captured the urgency and confusion inside the home as Haleigh’s family reported that the child could not be found.

Authorities quickly issued an Amber Alert. Haleigh was described as a white girl with blond hair and brown eyes who was about 3 feet tall and weighed roughly 39 pounds. She had distinctive medical and physical characteristics, including Turner syndrome, which can affect growth, and authorities circulated photographs and identifying information nationwide.

The alert triggered a large-scale search involving local deputies, state and federal authorities, volunteers, search dogs, divers and aircraft. Teams combed woods, waterways, roadsides and abandoned properties around Satsuma and elsewhere in Putnam County. Investigators also reviewed thousands of tips and interviewed relatives, neighbors, acquaintances and known offenders.

Croslin’s account became a central focus because she said she was the last person known to have seen Haleigh at home. Investigators questioned her repeatedly about the evening’s timeline and about inconsistencies they said emerged during interviews. Croslin maintained that she did not know what happened to the child. She was never charged in connection with Haleigh’s disappearance.

Investigators considered a wide range of possibilities, including an abduction by a stranger, involvement by someone familiar with the family and the possibility that Haleigh had been taken elsewhere after something happened inside the home. Detectives checked registered sex offenders in the region, investigated people linked to the family and followed tips naming various individuals. Searches were conducted at several locations, including areas near the St. Johns River, but no publicly identified search produced Haleigh’s remains or evidence sufficient to charge anyone.

The case drew intense national attention, and the lives of several people around Haleigh were scrutinized publicly. Authorities repeatedly cautioned that being interviewed or investigated did not make someone a suspect and that no person had been formally accused of causing the child’s disappearance.

In 2010, the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office said investigators believed Haleigh was likely dead and that the case was being treated as a homicide investigation. That assessment did not result in charges, and officials did not publicly disclose evidence establishing exactly when, where or how she may have died.

Croslin and Cummings were later convicted in an unrelated prescription-drug trafficking case. Those convictions were separate from the missing-child investigation and did not resolve what happened to Haleigh.

Over the years, detectives have continued to review tips, revisit interviews and examine possible suspects or persons of interest as new information has surfaced. Authorities have said the investigation remains open and that even a small detail—particularly one withheld at the time—could help establish Haleigh’s movements after she was last seen.

Haleigh would now be an adult. Her disappearance remains listed by law enforcement and missing-child organizations, and no one has been charged in connection with it. Authorities continue to ask anyone with credible information to contact the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office or the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children.
